hints: Start from atomic number 27 for Co and remember the order of filling is $4\text{s}$ before $3\text{d}$, but electrons are lost from $4\text{s}$ first when forming a $2+$ ion.
walkthrough:
Build the cobalt atom**
Cobalt has atomic number 27, so you place 27 electrons in order. Up to $1\text{s}^22\text{s}^22\text{p}^6$ is 10 electrons, then $3\text{s}^23\text{p}^6$ takes you to 18. You have 9 left. Fill $4\text{s}^2$ first, then the remaining 7 go into $3\text{d}$, giving $3\text{d}^74\text{s}^2$.

Form the $\text{Co}^{2+}$ ion**
When a transition metal forms a $2+$ ion it loses the $4\text{s}$ electrons first, not the $3\text{d}$ electrons, even though $4\text{s}$ filled first. So remove both $4\text{s}^2$ electrons from Co and you are left with $3\text{s}^23\text{p}^63\text{d}^7$ as the outer configuration.

hints: Recall the familiar colour of aqueous cobalt(II) salts in water before any chloride is added.
Think about what happens when a very high concentration of $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands competes with water as a ligand for $\text{Co}^{2+}$.
Write the formulae for the starting hexaaqua complex with coordination number 6 and the chloride complex with coordination number 4, checking the overall charges.
Recall the characteristic colour of the chloro complex of cobalt(II) often seen in the cobalt chloride test for water.
Link coordination number 6 to one common geometry and coordination number 4 with a large halide ligand to the other common geometry for cobalt(II).
walkthrough:
Picture the starting solution**
In aqueous $\text{Co}(\text{NO}_3)_2$, the $\text{Co}^{2+}$ is not free. Water acts as a ligand and surrounds it with six water molecules, forming $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$. This hexaaqua ion is very characteristic, it gives a pink solution.

See the ligand exchange**
Concentrated $\text{HCl}$ provides a huge excess of $\text{Cl}^-$ ions. Chloride can replace water as a ligand:
$$[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^- \rightleftharpoons [\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
So you move from an aqua complex to a chloro complex.

Link the new complex to its colour**
The product $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$ is intensely blue. That is why the pink solution turns blue as the equilibrium shifts to the right. This is the same colour change used in the test for water with blue cobalt chloride paper turning pink.

Assign the geometries**
Count the ligands. $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ has coordination number 6, which is octahedral. $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$ has coordination number 4. With the relatively large $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands around the small $\text{Co}^{2+}$, four ligands arrange tetrahedrally to minimise repulsion.

Summarise the observation**
Pink octahedral $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ changes to blue tetrahedral $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$ on adding conc. $\text{HCl(aq)}$. Colour comes from d-orbital splitting changing with ligand type and geometry.

Final answer: Initial solution is pink due to $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$, octahedral.
On addition of conc. $\text{HCl}$ it turns blue due to $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$, tetrahedral.

hints: Compare coordination number 4 geometries: think which geometry allows two different arrangements of two $\text{I}$ and two $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ ligands and which does not.
For the metal that shows two isomers, imagine placing the two identical ligands next to each other versus opposite each other in a plane.
For the metal that shows only one structure, imagine four different ligand positions at the corners of a tetrahedron where all positions are equivalent.
walkthrough:
Use the isomer count to deduce geometry**
Both formulae are $\text{M}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{I}_2$ with coordination number 4. Tetrahedral complexes of type $\text{MA}_2\text{B}_2$ have only one structure because every corner of a tetrahedron is adjacent to every other corner. Square planar complexes of type $\text{MA}_2\text{B}_2$ have two structures, cis and trans. Since Ni shows two isomers and Co shows one, Ni must be square planar and Co must be tetrahedral.

Draw the cobalt complex**
Put $\text{Co}$ in the centre and draw wedge and dashed bonds to show 3D tetrahedron. Attach $\text{I}$ to two corners and $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ to the other two corners. Any swapping gives the same structure, so only one diagram is needed.

Draw the two nickel isomers**
Put $\text{Ni}$ in the centre with four bonds in one plane. For cis-$\text{Ni}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{I}_2$, place the two $\text{I}$ ligands at $90^{\circ}$ to each other on adjacent corners, with the two $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ ligands also adjacent. For trans-$\text{Ni}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{I}_2$, place the two $\text{I}$ ligands at $180^{\circ}$ opposite each other, with the two $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ ligands also opposite.

Check your diagrams**
Label the central metal and each ligand clearly as $\text{I}$ or $\text{R}_3\text{P}$. Show tetrahedral with wedges for Co and flat cross shape for Ni to make the geometry obvious to the examiner.

Final answer: $\text{Co}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{I}_2$: tetrahedral with $\text{Co}$ at centre, $2 \times \text{I}$ and $2 \times \text{R}_3\text{P}$ at the four corners, only one arrangement possible.
$\text{Ni}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{I}_2$: square planar, two isomers: cis with $2 \times \text{I}$ adjacent ($90^{\circ}$ apart) and trans with $2 \times \text{I}$ opposite ($180^{\circ}$ apart).
